insight.title: Why Coins Have Ridges on the Edges
insight.subtitle: A clever trick invented by Sir Isaac Newton to stop medieval thieves still protects your spare change today.
insight.notificationHook: Why quarters have those tiny ridges

sections.text: Run your thumb along the edge of a quarter, and you will feel dozens of tiny ridges. They aren’t there for grip—they were designed by Sir Isaac Newton to catch thieves.
In the 1690s, criminals secretly shaved precious silver off the smooth edges of coins to melt down and sell. Newton, running the Royal Mint, added ridges so shaved coins were instantly spotted.

Today, coins are no longer made of precious metals, but governments kept the ridges. They help the visually impaired identify denominations and allow vending machines to verify authentic coins instantly.
Isaac Newton’s anti-theft design is still jingling in your pocket.
